passages.name: Continue
passages.source_raw: [img[img/town.webp]] As you slowly come to, you realize that you're in a small, unfamiliar town. You have no idea how you got there, but one thing is clear - your life has been turned upside down. In this new reality, you are nobody. You have no friends, no connections, and no one to rely on. With no other options, you must start from scratch and build a new life for yourself. You'll need to find a job to support yourself, a place to live, and maybe even make some new friends along the way. But be warned, this new world is filled with obstacles that you'll need to overcome. Can you adapt to this new life and find success, or will you fall victim to the challenges ahead? The choice is yours. Are you ready to take the first step into your [[new life?|newintro]]

passages.name: Help
passages.source_raw: !!FAQ If you'd rather connect with our community, chat and ask your questions there, you can do so here! [[Discord|https://discord.gg/rPSPtFhzAv]] If not, enjoy reading through this amazing FAQ, beautifully crafted and put together by Taulion! "How do I get a new job?" Remember that you're only allowed to have one job at a time! New job locations are unlocked as you play through the game. Currently, there's locations for jobs in almost any hub. Hubs are places with a lot of buildings, i.e the City, Uptown, Downtown, Streets and so forth. Check out the buildings while being unemployed to find new jobs. "My character is such a prude!" That's not a question, but you could try to lower her inhibition! "I've got no inhibition, how do I unlock more scenes?" Some content unlocks as you raise your other stats and make progress with the main questline. Some side-content requires additional items available in the mall. "How do the other stats work?" Corruption: This shows the current corruption of the character. It will increase with lewd acts, as well as open up for more scenes! Allure: This shows how much the character is desired by others. This will increase the chance of non consensual encounters! Arousal: This shows how much of a horndog you are. "Why can't I go to the alley or lake?" Explore the locations already available to you. There might be events that you've missed. Remember that some activities can be tried multiple times, and might change as you increase your stats. "How do I go on a date?" You can contact characters using a phone, available at the mall. Later, some dates can be started from a character's room. "I raised my relationship with a character, how do I progress further in this relationship?" You can only go on dates for now. More relationship content will be added in future updates! "How do I progess with story?" Story progresses itself rather autonomous, all you have to do is be available and talk to the characters that is guaranteed to come speak to you. Some parts of the story only trigger if you're in the right places, i.e the mansion or the Street. "I have unlocked the church, can I see the brothel, too?" The story is path determined, so no. You'll have to restart. "I'm trapped with Tim!" Too bad. ---- This game is currently in development, we announce new updates on our discord, and they can be downloaded at; [[F95Zone|https://f95zone.to/threads/new-life-project-v0-4-1a-nota-bao.158423/]] [[TFGames|https://www.tfgames.site/index.php?module=viewgame&id=3041]] Join the discord here! passages.name: downtownExplore
passages.source_raw:
[img[img/downtown.webp]]

<<if visited() is 1>>As you walk further downtown, you notice there's a club here, a mall, and a library. This place could be exciting. Neon lights flicker above the club entrance, distant music thumping through the walls like a heartbeat. The mall sprawls across a few blocks, its glass doors glinting in the afternoon sun, promising shops, food, and maybe answers. The library stands quiet and grand, ivy climbing its stone facade - a strange contrast to the rest of the street's energy.

Just past the corner, a small cinema marquee catches your eye. Its retro signage glows faintly, advertising movies you've never heard of. There's something oddly timeless about it, as if it hasn't changed in decades. You get the feeling each of these places holds a different kind of secret.

You pause, the streets unusually empty despite the signs of life. Where do you go first?<<elseif visited() is 2>>You stroll further into downtown. The club pulses faintly with music, its doors shut tight but vibrating with energy. The mall buzzes softly - not with crowds, but with electricity, lights flickering as if trying to remember their rhythm. The library looms nearby, its windows tinted too dark to see inside, yet you sense movement behind them. Just beyond, the cinema glows like an old memory, the posters outside faded but recent.

Every corner hums with the promise of something just out of sight.<<elseif visited() gte 3>>Downtown stretches out in front of you, strangely empty yet full of potential. The club's facade shimmers, catching your eye like it wants you to come closer. The mall's automatic doors slide open for no one, revealing shadowy halls lined with mannequins. The library stands silent, its tall glass doors locked - or maybe just pretending to be. The cinema's ticket booth is unattended, but the lights inside are on. A movie is playing.

You feel watched, but not unwelcome.<</if>>

[[Go back|exploreIntro]]

<<AdvancePeriod>><<replace "#now">><<now>><</replace>>

passages.name: uptownExplore
passages.source_raw:
[img[img/uptown.webp]]

<<if visited() is 1>>As you walk further uptown, you notice a bar, a beauty salon, and a car dealership. Perhaps some of those could come in handy at some point? The bar is tucked between two brick buildings, its sign half-lit and swaying slightly in the breeze - the kind of place where locals might trade stories... or secrets. The beauty salon next door gleams with soft lighting and the faint scent of hairspray and lavender drifting out when the door opens. It feels oddly pristine, like it's waiting for someone - maybe you.

Across the street, rows of shiny vehicles line the lot of a small car dealership. The place looks quiet, but not abandoned. A figure moves behind the tinted glass of the office. There's something about the way the cars reflect the sky - polished, but still... off.

Everything here seems useful, but nothing feels quite normal.

Where to next?<<elseif visited() is 2>>Uptown has a quieter pulse. The bar door creaks in the wind, though no one enters or leaves. Faint laughter echoes from within - or maybe it's just your imagination. The beauty salon is spotless, chairs lined up like soldiers. A hairdryer hums in the back, unattended. The car dealership glints in the sunlight, but the cars are all eerily identical, parked too precisely. Someone might be watching you from inside the office.

Nothing moves, but the place feels alive.<<elseif visited() gte 3>>You pass through uptown again. The bar's windows are fogged from the inside, hiding whatever's happening - or not happening - within. The beauty salon door is slightly ajar, the bell above it silent. A magazine flutters on the front desk, its pages turning on their own. The car dealership lot is full, but no cars seem to have left. The lights in the office flicker when you glance toward them.

It's as if the town's waiting for you to make the first move.<</if>>

[[Go back|exploreIntro]]

<<AdvancePeriod>><<replace "#now">><<now>><</replace>>

passages.source_raw:
!!Emergency Response

Managing Stroke Symptoms: Upon recognizing signs and symptoms of stroke in a patient (such as facial drooping, arm weakness, and slurred speech), the nurse quickly assesses the patient's neurological status using standardized stroke scales. They initiate a stroke alert, notify the stroke team, and prepare for urgent diagnostic imaging (e.g., CT scan) to determine eligibility for thrombolytic therapy or endovascular intervention.

Treating Anaphylaxis: When a patient develops signs of anaphylaxis (such as hives, swelling, difficulty breathing, and hypotension) after receiving a medication or exposure to an allergen, the nurse administers epinephrine promptly, initiates intravenous fluids, and prepares to manage airway compromise. They monitor the patient closely for signs of improvement or worsening and collaborate with the healthcare team to ensure appropriate follow-up care.

Responding to Seizures: Upon witnessing a patient experiencing a seizure, the nurse ensures the patient's safety by protecting their head from injury, maintaining a clear airway, and removing any nearby hazards. They time the seizure duration, assess for injuries or complications, and provide comfort and reassurance to the patient and their family. Post-seizure, the nurse monitors the patient for signs of postictal state and administers medications as prescribed to prevent further seizures.

Managing Respiratory Distress in Asthma: When a patient presents with severe respiratory distress due to an asthma exacerbation, the nurse assesses the severity of symptoms, administers nebulized bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol), and provides oxygen therapy to improve oxygenation. They monitor the patient's respiratory status, auscultate lung sounds for wheezing, and assess the effectiveness of treatment. If the patient's condition deteriorates, the nurse prepares for advanced interventions such as intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Addressing Hypoglycemia: Upon identifying a patient with symptomatic hypoglycemia (e.g., confusion, diaphoresis, tachycardia), the nurse assesses blood glucose levels using a glucometer and administers rapid-acting carbohydrates (e.g., oral glucose gel, intravenous dextrose) to raise blood sugar levels quickly. They monitor the patient's response to treatment, reassess blood glucose levels, and provide education on preventing future episodes of hypoglycemia.

Managing Cardiopulmonary Arrest: In the event of a cardiopulmonary arrest, the nurse follows the American Heart Association's Basic Life Support (BLS) and Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines to initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), provide defibrillation if indicated, and administer medications (e.g., epinephrine, amiodarone) as per protocol. They coordinate with the code team, delegate tasks, and ensure effective teamwork to optimize outcomes.

!!Hygiene

Remember to wash your hands thoroughly. Wash up towards elbow before drying off. Make sure anything you touch after this is sterile, and do not touch patient with hands unless it is necessary.

passages.name: fertLogs
passages.source_raw:
[img[img/fertLogs.webp]] You enter the server room to access the fertility research logs. Usually they won't let anyone in here to review them, but since your name is literally on almost every sign in this department, it would seem weird that you aren't allowed to enter here. You click on one of the files.
<><><>Fertility Log Review #12. Date: August 14, 2024 Subject: Age-related ovarian decline study (Female, 18) Procedure: Ovarian reserve testing using AMH and AFC markers. Results:
  • AMH levels at 0.8 ng/mL, indicating low ovarian reserve.
  • Antral follicle count (AFC) of 5.
    • Notes: Significant reduction in ovarian activity compared to previous tests conducted at age 35, suggesting accelerated decline in fertility. Next Steps: Consideration of egg freezing as a preventive measure before further reduction in ovarian reserve.<>Fertility Log Review #3. Date: September 2, 2024 Subject: Male infertility and sperm motility (Male, 25) Procedure: Semen analysis conducted following 3 months of dietary supplements aimed at improving sperm health. Results:
  • Sperm motility increased from 30% to 42%.
  • Total sperm count rose from 18 million to 22 million.
    • Notes: Modest improvement in sperm quality noted, though patient remains below the fertility threshold for conception without assistance. Next Steps: Continue supplements for another 3 months, review lifestyle factors (stress, diet).<>Fertility Log Review #4. Date: October 5, 2024 Subject: Impact of PCOS on ovulation cycles (Female, 19) Procedure: Clomiphene citrate (Clomid) trial to induce ovulation. Results:
  • Ovulation confirmed on Day 16 of the cycle.
  • Progesterone levels at 10 ng/mL post-ovulation, within acceptable range.
    • Notes: Ovulatory response to Clomid is positive, though concerns about thin endometrial lining (6mm). Next Steps: Evaluate potential for using Letrozole as an alternative ovulation induction medication.<>Fertility Log Review #16. Date: July 12, 2024 Subject: Unexplained infertility after 2 years of trying (Couple, F 18, M 19) Procedure: Diagnostic laparoscopy and hysteroscopy. Results:
  • No structural abnormalities in uterus or fallopian tubes.
  • Mild endometriosis (Stage 1) found but unlikely the primary cause of infertility.
    • Notes: Diagnosis of unexplained infertility upheld. Laparoscopic excision of endometriosis completed. Next Steps: Begin intrauterine insemination (IUI) protocol with ovarian stimulation.<>Fertility Log Review #21. Date: November 10, 2024 Subject: Egg quality preservation and IVF planning (Female, 21) Procedure: Egg retrieval for IVF following 10 days of ovarian stimulation. Results:
  • 12 eggs retrieved, 7 mature, 5 fertilized successfully.
  • Embryos developing normally at Day 3.
    • Notes: Good initial response to stimulation given patient's age. Will proceed with preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) for chromosomal normalcy. Next Steps: Embryo transfer scheduled for next cycle.<>Fertility Log Review #3. Date: August 25, 2024 Subject: Male fertility recovery post-chemotherapy (Male, 24) Procedure: Sperm banking after 12 months post-chemotherapy for Hodgkin's lymphoma. Results:
  • Sperm count low (6 million), motility also reduced at 22%.
    • Notes: Chemotherapy has clearly impacted fertility, but sperm production persists at a reduced rate. Next Steps: Recommend further sperm banking and consultation with reproductive urologist.<>Fertility Log Review #7. Date: June 30, 2024 Subject: Ovulation tracking post-miscarriage (Female, 20) Procedure: Monitoring ovulation using basal body temperature (BBT) and luteinizing hormone (LH) strips. Results:
  • Ovulation confirmed on Day 14 based on LH surge and BBT rise.
  • Progesterone levels after ovulation in normal range (12 ng/mL).
    • Notes: Patient's cycle returned to normal range 2 months after miscarriage, with healthy luteal phase indicators. Next Steps: Continue natural conception attempts for 6 months before considering assisted reproductive technologies.<>Fertility Log Review #18. Date: September 14, 2024 Subject: Donor egg IVF for early menopause (Female, 26) Procedure: Egg donor selection and synchronization of cycles for embryo transfer. Results:
  • 10 donor eggs received, 8 fertilized, 6 viable blastocysts at Day 5.
    • Notes: Excellent embryo development; donor quality confirmed. Recipient endometrial lining at 8.5mm, suitable for implantation. Next Steps: Proceed with embryo transfer after PGT results.<>Fertility Log Review #24. Date: December 1, 2024 Subject: Impact of lifestyle changes on fertility (Couple, F 21, M 22) Procedure: Review after 6 months of targeted lifestyle changes (diet, exercise, cessation of alcohol/smoking). Results:
  • Female: Improved AMH levels from 1.1 ng/mL to 1.6 ng/mL.
  • Male: Sperm mobility increased to 52%, count up to 30 million.
    • Notes: Significant positive outcomes from lifestyle interventions, particularly for male partner. Next Steps: Begin IUI with ovarian stimulation in next cycle.<>Fertility Log Review #27. Date: March 7, 2024 Subject: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) and IVF outcomes (Female, 18) Procedure: IVF stimulation cycle using gonadotropins. Results:
  • 18 eggs retrieved, 10 mature, 6 fertilized.
  • 3 viable blastocysts on Day 5, poor embryo quality noted in remaining samples.
    • Notes: High response to stimulation but concerns about overall embryo quality. PCOS likely influencing egg quality. Next Steps: Consider mild IVF protocol for future cycles to improve egg quality and embryo viability.<    ><    >
    Very interesting information. Although, you can't really use this information for anything. [[Leave|fertRes]]

passages.name: honeySpeak
passages.source_raw:
[img[img/honeyFarms.webp]]

You strike up a conversation with one of the rooftop farmhands overlooking the sprawl of Los Huevas.

He leans on a raised planter, hands still dusted with soil, and tells you about the philosophy behind their work. It's not just about growing food, he explains - it's about rebuilding a relationship between people and the environment, even in a concrete city.

They focus on ethical farming practices: no synthetic pesticides, water conservation systems, and crop rotation designed to keep the soil healthy year-round. He gestures to a corner where compost bins hum quietly and pollinator plants draw bees from nearby rooftop hives.

“This isn't industrial agriculture,” he says, wiping sweat from his brow. “This is something closer to stewardship. Every plant, every system we build here, is part of a cycle - and we're just one part of it.”

He tells you how rooftop farms like this one not only provide fresh produce to the local community but also create green spaces that cool buildings, absorb carbon, and remind people that food doesn't have to come from a truck 500 miles away.

It's a quiet, deliberate kind of work. And the way he talks about it, it almost sounds like a calling.

You walk away with a new respect for the patchwork of green stitched above the city.

[[Leave|honeyFarms]]

[img[img/jobClass.webp]] <><>As you step into the classroom, a wave of noise hits you. Students chatter loudly, some with their feet propped on desks, while others scroll through their phones, completely ignoring your arrival. A group in the back is tossing paper balls at each other, and a pair near the window is deep in conversation about last night's game. The hum of conversation and laughter drowns out your thoughts as you contemplate how to restore order.<>The classroom is unnervingly quiet as you enter. All eyes turn toward you as the students sit up straight, hands neatly folded on their desks. Not a single phone or whisper in sight. It feels almost too perfect. Today's lesson: <><>The Skeletal System: Structure and Function Overview: The skeletal system provides structure, support, and protection for the body. This lesson covers the major bones, their organization, and their functions, emphasizing how they enable movement and protect vital organs. Key Concepts:
  • Structure and functions of the skeletal system (support, protection, movement)
  • Major bones in the body (e.g., skull, spine, ribcage, pelvis, arms, and legs)
  • Different types of joints (ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot) and their role in movement
    • Activities:
    1. Bone Labeling Exercise: Label a skeletal diagram with major bones and learn their names and functions.
    2. Joint Movement Exploration: Observe and move different joints (e.g., shoulder, knee) to understand how joint types affect movement.
    3. Build-a-Bone Model: Create a simple bone model, demonstrating its structure and how it connects to other bones.
    <>The Muscular System: Movement and Control Overview: Muscles work in pairs to create movement and maintain posture. This lesson explores major muscle groups, types of muscle tissue, and how muscles interact with the skeletal system for movement. Key Concepts:
  • Types of muscles (skeletal, cardiac, and smooth) and their roles
  • Major muscle groups (e.g., biceps, triceps, quadriceps) and their locations
  • How muscles contract and relax to produce movement
    • Activities:
    1. Muscle Mapping: Label and color the major muscle groups on a diagram to understand their placement and function.
    2. Flex and Extend Activity: Perform simple exercises (like bicep curls) to observe muscle contraction and relaxation.
    3. Muscle Model Creation: Use clay to build a model showing how muscles attach to bones to facilitate movement.
    <>The Circulatory System: Heart and Blood Vessels Overview: The circulatory system is responsible for transporting oxygen, nutrients, and waste products throughout the body. This lesson introduces the structure of the heart, blood vessels, and the pathway of blood circulation. Key Concepts:
  • Parts of the heart (e.g., atria, ventricles, valves) and their functions
  • Types of blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) and their roles in circulation
  • The path of blood flow through the body (systemic and pulmonary circuits)
    • Activities:
    1. Heart Diagram Labeling: Label a heart diagram with its main parts and trace the path of blood through the chambers.
    2. Pulse Activity: Measure and compare pulse rates at rest and after exercise to observe how heart rate changes.
    3. Circulation Model: Create a simple model using tubing and colored water to demonstrate blood flow through arteries and veins.
    <>The Respiratory System: Breathing and Gas Exchange Overview: The respiratory system allows for the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the body. This lesson explores the pathway of air, major respiratory organs, and how breathing works. Key Concepts:
  • Structure and function of respiratory organs (e.g., nose, trachea, lungs, diaphragm)
  • The process of gas exchange in the alveoli
  • Mechanics of breathing (inhalation and exhalation)
    • Activities:
    1. Respiratory System Diagram: Label the parts of the respiratory system on a diagram, from the nose to the lungs.
    2. Breathing Experiment: Observe and measure breaths per minute at rest and after physical activity to see how breathing rate changes.
    3. Lung Model Creation: Build a simple lung model using a balloon and plastic bottle to show how the diaphragm moves during breathing.

[img[img/jobClass.webp]] You tell the class to pick up their biology books. It's time for a lesson in the wonderful arts of biological advancement! Today's lesson: <><>Cell Structure and Function Overview: Cells are the basic units of life, responsible for carrying out essential processes that sustain life. This lesson will explore cell types, organelles, and their functions. Key Concepts:
  • Differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
  • Functions of cell organelles (e.g., nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes)
  • Cell membrane structure and transport mechanisms (osmosis, diffusion)
    • Activities:
    1. Microscope Lab: Observe prepared slides of plant and animal cells to identify organelles.
    2. Cell Model Creation: Build a 3D model of a eukaryotic cell, labeling each organelle and its function.
    3. Interactive Diagram Labeling: Use an online tool to label cell parts and receive feedback.
    <>Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration Overview: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are key metabolic processes that provide energy for life. This lesson will investigate how plants and animals convert energy for growth and survival. Key Concepts:
  • Photosynthesis equation and stages (light-dependent and Calvin cycle)
  • Cellular respiration stages (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain)
  • Energy flow and ATP production
    • Activities:
    1. Plant Leaf Experiment: Test the presence of starch in leaves using iodine to show the end product of photosynthesis.
    2. Breathing and Exercise Lab: Measure changes in breathing rate to illustrate cellular respiration in action.
    3. Flowchart Creation: Students create a flowchart showing energy conversion in photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
    <>Genetics and Heredity Overview: This lesson introduces students to the principles of inheritance and the role of DNA in passing traits from parents to offspring. It will cover Mendelian genetics, Punnett squares, and the structure of DNA. Key Concepts:
  • Mendelian inheritance (dominant, recessive traits)
  • Punnett squares for predicting genotype and phenotype probabilities
  • DNA structure and function in heredity
    • Activities:
    1. Punnett Square Practice: Solve genetic cross problems to predict inheritance patterns.
    2. DNA Extraction Lab: Extract DNA from strawberries or other fruits to observe genetic material.
    3. Family Trait Analysis: Chart and analyze simple traits (like eye color or tongue rolling) within students' families.
    <>Ecosystems and Energy Flow Overview: Ecosystems are complex networks of organisms interacting with each other and their environment. This lesson focuses on food chains, energy flow, and the interdependence of organisms within an ecosystem. Key Concepts:
  • Trophic levels and roles (producers, consumers, decomposers)
  • Energy flow in food chains and food webs
  • Ecological balance and human impact on ecosystems
    • Activities:
    1. Food Web Creation: Students draw food webs for different ecosystems, identifying primary producers, consumers, and decomposers.
    2. Energy Pyramid Lab: Build a physical or virtual energy pyramid to illustrate energy loss at each trophic level.
    3. Ecosystem Simulation: Use a digital simulation tool to see how changes in one species affect the entire ecosystem.
    <>Human Body Systems Overview: The human body is composed of complex systems that work together to maintain homeostasis. This lesson will focus on major systems (circulatory, respiratory, digestive, nervous) and how they support human life. Key Concepts:
  • Structure and function of the circulatory, respiratory, digestive, and nervous systems
  • Interdependence of body systems for maintaining homeostasis
  • Common disorders and diseases affecting each system
    • Activities:
    1. Heart Rate Investigation: Measure heart rate before and after exercise to understand circulatory and respiratory responses.
    2. Digestive System Diagram: Label the parts of the digestive system and trace the path food takes through it.
    3. Interactive Body System Quiz: Test knowledge with a quiz matching organs to their systems and functions.

Today's lesson: <><>Basic Algebra: Understanding Variables and Expressions Overview: Algebra introduces the use of symbols and letters to represent numbers and values in mathematical expressions and equations.   • Definition and role of variables

    • Activities:

    3. Solve and Check: Solve simple equations and verify the answers by substituting the solution back into the original equation.
    <>Geometry: Exploring Shapes and Angles Overview: Geometry is the study of shapes, their properties, and spatial relationships. This lesson introduces basic shapes, types of angles, and angle relationships. Key Concepts:
  • Properties of basic shapes (triangles, quadrilaterals, circles)
  • Types of angles (acute, obtuse, right)
  • Angle relationships (complementary, supplementary, and vertical angles)
    • Activities:
    1. Shape Identification: Sort and classify various shapes based on their properties.
    2. Angle Measurement Lab: Use a protractor to measure angles in different shapes and identify angle types.
    3. Angle Sum Exploration: Discover the sum of angles in triangles and quadrilaterals by drawing and measuring angles.
    <>Fractions and Decimals: Understanding Parts of a Whole Overview: Fractions and decimals represent parts of a whole and are fundamental in various areas of math. This lesson will help students understand how to convert, compare, and perform basic operations with fractions and decimals. Key Concepts:
  • Converting between fractions and decimals
  • Comparing and ordering fractions and decimals
  • Adding and subtracting fractions with like and unlike denominators
    • Activities:
    1. Fraction-Decimal Conversion Practice: Convert given fractions into decimals and vice versa.
    2. Fraction Ordering Game: Arrange fractions and decimals from smallest to largest on a number line.
    3. Fraction Operations Lab: Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with different denominators using visual aids.
    <>Introduction to Probability and Statistics Overview: Probability and statistics help us analyze patterns and make predictions. This lesson introduces the basic principles of probability, data collection, and data representation. Key Concepts:
  • Basic probability (likelihood of events)
  • Collecting and organizing data (e.g., through surveys or experiments)
  • Representing data in charts and graphs (bar graphs, line plots)
    • Activities:
    1. Coin Toss Experiment: Calculate the probability of heads or tails by tossing a coin and recording results.
    2. Data Collection Activity: Conduct a small survey, collect data, and represent it in a bar or pie chart.
    3. Probability Scenarios: Determine probabilities of various outcomes in real-world scenarios (e.g., rolling dice, picking cards).
    <>Introduction to Algebraic Functions and Graphs Overview: Algebraic functions and graphs allow us to visualize relationships between variables. This lesson introduces linear functions, graphing points, and interpreting graphs. Key Concepts:
  • Understanding functions and their notation
  • Plotting points on a coordinate plane
  • Graphing linear functions and identifying slope and intercepts
    • Activities:
    1. Coordinate Plane Plotting: Plot given points on a coordinate plane and connect them to form a shape or line.
    2. Graphing Linear Functions: Graph linear equations by finding the slope and y-intercept.
    3. Function Machine Activity: Use a "function machine" to see how input changes output, identifying linear patterns.

Thank you for joining me tonight. I want you to close your eyes for a moment. Imagine the stories that shaped your childhood-the myths, legends, the whispered tales your grandparents told you, the heroes you looked up to. Every culture, every family, every individual carries stories. Professor Miller: They're more than entertainment; they are identity, wisdom, and warnings from those who came before us. In our lecture tonight, we'll unravel why these stories, from ancient myth to modern folklore, have such power. By the end, I hope you'll see how each tale we hold dear changes not just us, but our communities, and even our world. Professor Miller: Will you join me in this exploration? He then proceeds with the class. With power comes responsibility-our responsibility. How do we ensure that we do not repeat mistakes from the past? That we understand the ethical boundaries of human creation? Professor Everett: I invite you to look closer with me, to understand why each piece, no matter how small, matters in the web of life. She then continues with the class. How does choice impact our happiness, our identity, and our society? We'll explore these questions from a philosophical perspective tonight, drawing on thinkers from ancient Greece to modern psychology. passages.name: silvergateRestaurant
passages.source_raw: You step through the grand double doors into a world of quiet elegance. The air is hushed, the lighting soft and golden, casting gentle shadows on white-linen tables and glinting glassware. Crystal chandeliers shimmer above like frozen fireworks. Every surface gleams. A well-dressed waiter approaches with practiced grace, offering a polite nod as if you've been expected. The scent of truffle oil and aged wine lingers in the air-expensive, unmistakable. This is no ordinary restaurant. This is a place where silence speaks of wealth, and every detail whispers luxury. Bartholomew: Good evening. May I help you? @@.you;$name: Yes... I was hoping to be seated.@@ Bartholomew: Of course. May I see your credentials? <>@@.you;$name: I... wasn't aware they were needed.@@ Bartholomew: They always are. @@.you;$name: I've heard wonderful things. I came a long way...@@ Bartholomew: I don't doubt your intentions. But here, intention is not admission. You understand. @@.you;$name: There's no exception?@@ Bartholomew: None. This place is not for everyone. It never was. A pause hangs between you. Bartholomew gestures delicately toward the exit. Bartholomew: Should circumstances change... we will remember your face. [[Hotel Celestine->silvergateHotel]] [[Exit the restaurant|silvergate]]<> [[Hotel Celestine->silvergateHotel]] [[Exit the restaurant|silvergate]]<>

passages.name: scienceClassmateConvo
passages.source_raw: <><>@@.you;$name: If atoms are mostly empty space, then am I really as solid as I think I am?@@ $classmateName: Maybe you're more of a suggestion than an actual object. @@.you;$name: That's deep... or just deeply unsettling.@@<>@@.you;$name: You ever wonder if we're all just the universe's way of looking at itself?@@ $classmateName: You think the universe is some kind of narcissist? @@.you;$name: It wouldn't be the first one to make everything about itself.@@<>$classmateName: If humans are technically animals, does that mean we're just overcomplicated pets? @@.you;$name: Pretty much. Except, we're the ones who feed ourselves and clean up after ourselves.@@<>@@.you;$name: If I'm made of stardust, does that mean my life is written in the stars?@@ $classmateName: Well, you do have a habit of staring at the sky and daydreaming, so maybe. @@.you;$name: I'm just trying to figure out how to get to the stars...or at least the snack aisle.@@<>@@.you;$name: What if I told you the moon was just a big floating mirror?@@ $classmateName: I'd tell you to stop watching sci-fi movies. @@.you;$name: You can't tell me that wouldn't be kind of cool though!@@<>@@.you;$name: Did you know you could technically be immortal if you just kept cloning yourself?@@ $classmateName: Wouldn't that just be creepy? Like, you'd never be able to escape your own weirdness. @@.you;$name: It'd be like living in an episode of Black Mirror.@@<>@@.you;$name: If all life on Earth started from a single cell, can we really blame the first cell for all of this?@@ $classmateName: Blame it all on the first cell. It had no idea what it was doing. @@.you;$name: It just wanted a little company. Now look where we are-failing at science class.@@<>@@.you;$name: You ever think that maybe we just live in a simulation?@@ $classmateName: If this is a simulation, I want a better Wi-Fi connection. @@.you;$name: The only thing I want to change is the amount of sleep I'm getting.@@<>@@.you;$name: If humans evolved from monkeys, then why do we still have monkeys?@@ $classmateName: You can't just get rid of a whole species because we got fancy brains. @@.you;$name: Fair point. They do look pretty chill compared to us.@@<>@@.you;$name: So, if everything in the universe is made of atoms, does that mean we're all connected?@@ $classmateName: If we're all connected, does that mean I'm responsible for your weird thoughts? @@.you;$name: Absolutely. Just take the credit.@@<>@@.you;$name: Can we all agree that science has made us overthink way too many things?@@ $classmateName: 100%. But also, science is the reason I know pizza is technically a vegetable. @@.you;$name: Now *that's* the kind of science I can get behind.@@<>@@.you;$name: If the human body is 60% water, why am I still so thirsty all the time?@@ $classmateName: Because your brain is telling you you're thirsty, but your body is probably fine. @@.you;$name: My body might be fine, but my brain is definitely confused.@@<>@@.you;$name: If oxygen is so important for life, why does it also age us?@@ $classmateName: It's like oxygen is a bad friend who gets you into trouble. @@.you;$name: Oxygen is the friend that gets you to stay up late and then leaves you with bags under your eyes.@@<>@@.you;$name: I swear, atoms are just the universe's Lego pieces.@@ $classmateName: I mean, if you put enough of them together, you get cool stuff, like cars and buildings. @@.you;$name: And sometimes, you get an existential crisis.@@<>@@.you;$name: I bet the first person to discover fire was just trying to light a candle and got really lucky.@@ $classmateName: Honestly, probably. Just one too many sparks. @@.you;$name: One small spark, one giant leap for mankind.@@<>@@.you;$name: If light travels at the speed of light, does that mean it's the fastest thing in the universe?@@ $classmateName: I'd say it's the Usain Bolt of the universe. @@.you;$name: I just need that kind of speed to get through this class.@@<>@@.you;$name: Does gravity get tired of pulling stuff down all the time?@@ $classmateName: Nah, gravity's like that one friend who's always ready to help carry stuff. @@.you;$name: It's loyal, I'll give it that.@@<>@@.you;$name: If a tree falls in the forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound?@@ $classmateName: If no one is around, does it even fall? @@.you;$name: Philosophical, but I still want to know if it makes noise.@@<>@@.you;$name: You know how humans use tools? I wonder if ants have their own version of a "toolbox."@@ $classmateName: I bet they have little ant-sized hammers and screwdrivers. @@.you;$name: And a tiny, tiny IKEA manual.@@<>@@.you;$name: Do you think we'll ever get to the point where we can send people to Mars and they won't immediately panic?@@ $classmateName: Maybe in a few hundred years, but I'm still trying to get through this class without panicking. @@.you;$name: Mars, or physics?@@ $classmateName: Both, honestly.<>

passages.name: physicsClassmateConvo
passages.source_raw: <><>@@.you;$name: If time is relative, does that mean I can be late and call it “time dilation”?@@ $classmateName: I'd love that excuse for my own lateness. @@.you;$name: It's the *only* excuse that makes sense.@@<>@@.you;$name: Why is gravity always pulling things down? What did we ever do to gravity?@@ $classmateName: Gravity's just doing its job. It's like that one friend who always keeps you grounded. @@.you;$name: It's the *worst* friend at parties though.@@<>@@.you;$name: If light travels at the speed of light, does that mean it's in a constant rush to get somewhere?@@ $classmateName: Yep, light's basically always running late to the party. @@.you;$name: And never gets caught in traffic. Lucky.@@<>@@.you;$name: Do you think the universe is ever bored just sitting there, doing nothing?@@ $classmateName: It's probably just chilling, waiting for someone to ask the big questions. @@.you;$name: It's got *eternity* to kill, right?@@<>@@.you;$name: If two objects collide in space and nobody is around to hear it, does it make a sound?@@ $classmateName: No, it's space. It's basically the universe's silent disco. @@.you;$name: That's a really *loud* way of saying "no" though.@@<>@@.you;$name: If black holes suck everything in, does that mean they're just super *hungry*?@@ $classmateName: Yeah, they're basically the universe's vacuum cleaner. @@.you;$name: A vacuum cleaner with no off switch.@@<>@@.you;$name: If atoms are mostly empty space, how come we can't just walk through walls?@@ $classmateName: You're asking the real questions now. I'd love to walk through walls. @@.you;$name: I'd settle for just being able to avoid traffic.@@<>@@.you;$name: What if gravity just decided to stop working for a day? What would happen?@@ $classmateName: I'm pretty sure we'd all go flying into space. @@.you;$name: That sounds terrifying... but kind of fun?@@<>@@.you;$name: If space is infinite, does that mean there are infinite versions of me somewhere out there?@@ $classmateName: There's definitely an alternate universe where you're still in bed, not doing physics homework. @@.you;$name: That sounds like *the* universe I want to be in.@@<>@@.you;$name: So if the speed of light is constant, does that mean it's always *on time*?@@ $classmateName: I guess light's never late to the party! @@.you;$name: Unlike the rest of us, who always seem to run into traffic.@@<>@@.you;$name: What if our entire reality is just a big experiment for some other civilization?@@ $classmateName: I'd like to think of it as *the* reality show of the universe. @@.you;$name: And we're all contestants, just waiting for the plot twist.@@<>@@.you;$name: Why are we taught that the universe is expanding, but it *feels* like everything is getting smaller?@@ $classmateName: Maybe it's all part of the grand cosmic joke. The universe's *expansion* is just slow motion. @@.you;$name: And we're the ones who can't catch up.@@<>@@.you;$name: You think quantum mechanics is just physics trying to confuse us on purpose?@@ $classmateName: I'm convinced quantum mechanics is just *chaos* pretending to be science. @@.you;$name: Chaos with a PhD, apparently.@@<>@@.you;$name: If energy can't be created or destroyed, does that mean I'm just recycling the same tired thoughts every day?@@ $classmateName: That's a pretty accurate description of my entire existence. @@.you;$name: I guess we're just energy in motion... but, like, a very tired motion.@@<>@@.you;$name: If gravity exists because of mass, does that mean small things don't have gravity?@@ $classmateName: I think small things have *tiny* gravity. @@.you;$name: Aww, little baby gravity. So cute.@@<>@@.you;$name: If everything in the universe is made of atoms, does that mean we're all basically just Lego blocks?@@ $classmateName: Except with way more drama. @@.you;$name: I don't think my Lego set ever made me question my life choices.@@<>@@.you;$name: What if time was just a big cosmic illusion and we were all stuck in an eternal “now”?@@ $classmateName: Time is definitely messing with us. I mean, why do Mondays feel so long? @@.you;$name: Time's got some serious issues with perception.@@<>@@.you;$name: If we know that the universe is expanding, where exactly is it expanding *into*?@@ $classmateName: That's like asking where the edge of the internet is. We might never know. @@.you;$name: The universe is a giant mystery box. No one has the instructions.@@<>@@.you;$name: If we could travel faster than light, would we be able to go back in time?@@ $classmateName: I think we'd break the universe if we tried. @@.you;$name: And probably cause a paradox. No thanks.@@<>@@.you;$name: Do you think black holes are just the universe's way of hiding its secrets?@@ $classmateName: I imagine black holes are like the universe's "Do Not Enter" sign. @@.you;$name: And yet, we still try to peek in. We just can't resist a good mystery.@@<>
